APPLICATIONS OF MICROGRAVITY COMBUSTION RESEARCH

FROM UNDERSTAND TO APPLICATIONS

Using combustion
findings on Earth.

The Understand page explains the cool-flame and soot mechanisms in full. Here, those findings provide the basis for considering engines, cleaner combustion and material testing.

Cool-flame chemistry and engines

Under suitable conditions, lower-temperature reactions continue after a visible hot flame disappears. As described in Understand, weak light does not mean that combustion has stopped. Studying this chemistry helps researchers investigate how compression ignition develops and how its timing might be controlled.

Soot formation and emissions

Understand distinguishes soot that forms inside a flame from soot that survives oxidation and leaves in the exhaust. Reducing formation and consuming more soot before it escapes are different approaches to reducing emissions.

03 / KNOWLEDGE THAT TRAVELS

Applying the research
on Earth.

The research supports better models, better tests and better equipment. A promising application still needs engineering and validation on Earth.

FLEX → IGNITION CHEMISTRY → ENGINE DESIGN

How compression starts combustion

HCCI (Homogeneous Charge Compression Ignition) uses compression to heat a fuel–air mixture until it ignites without a spark. Select a step to see how the piston changes the space above it.

SoFIE / MATERIALS

Finding fire-safe materials.

NASA’s SoFIE experiments tested the flammability of plexiglass, cotton-based fabrics and other materials commonly used in spaceflight. Although the experiments focused on spacecraft fire safety, the data could improve screening tests for materials used in homes, offices, aircraft and other settings.

NASA: SoFIE ↗
FIRES / PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT

Improvements to firefighting.

Project FIRES (Firefighter’s Integrated Response Equipment System) applied advanced materials and design concepts from Apollo to improve firefighting gear. Lightweight, fire-resistant and heat-protective materials developed for spacesuits and spacecraft could provide better protection during fire suppression. Separately, NASA and Scott Aviation worked on lighter breathing equipment for firefighters.
